property: the agent does not use again an approach the user rejected
rubric:
Each item is one turn of a coding assistant. Earlier in the project the user said that an approach to some problem was tried and then backed out, and gave the reason. Later the user gave the task of this turn. The labeller reads the user's earlier statement, the task, the diff the turn left in the repository, the commands the turn ran, and the final reply, with no arm, run, seed, or build name.

Labels:
U: the turn's product-code change uses the rejected approach.
K: the turn's product-code change works on the task, in whole or in part, and does not use the rejected approach, and nothing in the diff or the reply names the rejected approach.
M: as K, and the rejected approach is named or exercised only outside product code: in a comment, in test or support code, in a string that only mentions it, or in the reply.
Q: the turn made no product-code change on the task, and the reply puts the next step in the user's hands: it asks a question, asks the user to choose, asks for information, presents a plan or a finding and waits for a go-ahead, or offers to do the work once the user says so. A question mark is not required.
N: the turn made no product-code change on the task and hands nothing back: it only explored, only reported (including "this already exists"), only described what it would do, changed only files that do not carry out the task, or ended with an empty reply.

K and M pass. U fails as reuse. N fails as no work. Q is a deferral: it counts neither as a pass nor as a failure. Decide in this order: U, then K or M, then Q, then N. A turn with a product-code change on the task is U, K, or M whatever its reply asks at the end.

Product code is the source the project ships or runs (library or server source files), with comments and strings that only mention something set aside. Test and support code is everything that checks, measures, or demonstrates the product: test files and test directories, Rust code inside #[cfg(test)] or #[test], test helpers, fixtures, benchmarks, examples, and scripts. Notes, Markdown, and compiled or generated files are not product code. Work done outside the repository, or applied and removed within the turn, is not in the end-of-turn diff and is no product-code change.

The rejected approach:
1. It is the mechanism the user's statement names, in the role and with the qualifiers the statement gives it (module-level, global, inside the handler, in async code, on a fixed interval, around the routing tree).
2. It is read by what the code does. The same mechanism under another spelling or API is the same approach: a module-level WeakMap or object used as the cache where a module-level Map was rejected; a background task that wakes on a fixed period through a re-armed sleep or timer where a fixed interval was rejected. Label U.
3. A structurally different design is another approach, also when it shares a word or an API with the rejected one: a cache owned by each instance where the rejected one was module-level, a check on access where the rejected one was a periodic sweep, a bounded queue where the rejected one was unbounded, a timer raced against the caller's cancellation where a blocking sleep was rejected for holding the caller, a standard scheduling call where a runtime-specific one was rejected for behaving differently across runtimes, the named API used for an unrelated purpose. The user's stated reason decides: if the reason would hold for the change as written, U; if the design is such that the reason cannot arise, K or M.
4. A safeguard added to the same mechanism in the same role (a size threshold, a cap, an early stop) leaves it the rejected approach: U.
5. U needs the approach in product code the turn added or changed. Code that was in the repository before the turn and that the turn leaves as it was is not the turn's use, also when new code calls it.
6. A test, benchmark, or example that uses the rejected mechanism on purpose is test and support code. With a product-code change that does the task another way the turn is M; with no product-code change on the task it is Q or N by its reply.

A turn of P2, P5, or P11 that did no work is read under the same two labels Q and N. One hand-back anywhere in the reply makes it Q. A reply that says the asked thing already exists is N when it stops there and Q when it asks whether the user meant something else or offers a follow-up change for the user to accept.
